title: Mississippi mayor argues against lowering American flag for Dolly Parton after her death
text:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.

See more of our coverage in your search results.

A Mississippi mayor is facing backlash after defying President Trump’s directive to lower American flags Dolly Parton’s death.

“I believe lowering the American flag to half-staff should mean something very significant,” Mayor Ken Adams of Olive Branch, a suburb of Memphis, Tennessee, wrote on the city’s Facebook page on Friday.

“In my opinion, it should be reserved for our military heroes, fallen first responders, presidents and other major national leaders, or events that have had a tremendous impact on our country,” added the Republican mayor.

“If we lower the flag every time a well-known or beloved person passes away, I believe we eventually lessen the meaning of the gesture,” he wrote.

Adams, previously a DeSoto County judge and longtime FedEx executive, added that there was “no question” that the “Jolene” singer was a great person who brought happiness to millions and accomplished “tremendous things” in her life.

“I have nothing but respect for her,” he said in the post.

Adams cited Home Rule, which gives Mississippi cities the right to control their internal affairs, adding that he believes mayors should “use our own judgment when appropriate” and make decisions for their own constituents.

Both President Trump and Mississippi Gov. Tate Reeves ordered US and state flags flown at half-staff for one week following the country icon’s death on Tuesday at age 80.

Mayor Adams’ post was bombarded with comments after it was shared, with some pointing to flags in Olive Branch previously being lowered for both the death of Turning Point USA founder Charlie Kirk in 2025 and comedian Bob Hope in 2003.

Others pointed to Parton’s steadfast support for US military service members and multiple Presidential Medal of Freedom awards — all of which she declined.

“I’d lower it for Dolly before any politician,” one comment read.

“She did more for children than any politician ever has. That should raise her status in your eyes from ‘just a celebrity,'” wrote a second, citing Parton’s work delivering 270 million books to children in the US and abroad.

Others took a more nuanced view.

“Honestly i love Dolly Parton and I was a little dismayed when I saw you hadn’t lowered them but at the same time, as a veteran, I understand your point and I agree with you. May Dolly rest in grace,” wrote a third.
